name: SEWB Framework
what: The Social and Emotional Wellbeing (SEWB) framework is a multidimensional, holistic framework for wellbeing developed specifically for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. It encompasses seven interconnected dimensions and acknowledges the role of social, historical, and political determinants.
why: The SEWB framework represents a distinct and culturally grounded approach to understanding wellbeing that extends well beyond Western psychological models. It is directly specified in the VCE study design and must be understood both in its structure and its cultural significance.

items.title: I can define the SEWB framework and explain what makes it multidimensional and holistic
items.what: The SEWB framework is a framework for wellbeing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples that includes all elements of being. Multidimensional means it is made up of different components. Holistic means it considers the whole person, including mental, physical, spiritual, and social needs.
items.why: These two terms are specifically defined in the study design and are commonly tested. Students who conflate them or use them interchangeably will lose marks.
items.example: The SEWB framework is holistic because it does not treat mental health as separate from physical health, spiritual connection, or community. It is multidimensional because it identifies seven distinct sources of wellbeing, each of which contributes to the whole.

items.title: I can identify and describe each of the seven dimensions of the SEWB framework
items.what: The seven dimensions are: Connection to Body, Connection to Mind and Emotions, Connection to Family and Kinship, Connection to Community, Connection to Culture, Connection to Country, and Connection to Spirituality and Ancestors. Each is interconnected and contributes to overall wellbeing.
items.why: Exam questions can ask students to identify specific dimensions or apply them to scenarios. Knowing all seven dimensions and their meanings is essential.
items.example: An Elder passing traditional language and ceremonial knowledge to younger community members addresses the Culture dimension. A community health worker visiting an isolated family member addresses the Community dimension.

items.title: I can explain what Connection to Country means in the context of the SEWB framework
items.what: Country refers to the traditional lands of a particular language or cultural group, encompassing not only geographical boundaries but also the spiritual, emotional, and intellectual connections to and within those lands. In this framework, people belong to the land rather than owning it.
items.why: This concept is frequently misunderstood as simply referring to a geographic location. Understanding its cultural and spiritual depth is important for respectful and accurate exam responses.
items.example: An Aboriginal person who is displaced from their ancestral land and unable to participate in land-based cultural practices may experience reduced wellbeing in the Connection to Country dimension, affecting their overall SEWB.

items.title: I can explain what Connection to Spirituality and Ancestors means in the SEWB framework
items.what: Spirituality in this framework is a concept that connects all things and shapes beliefs, values, and behaviour. Ancestors are understood as interconnected with Creation spirits and Country, watching over, guiding, and protecting families and communities. This creates a sense of purpose and wellbeing.
items.why: This dimension is distinct from how spirituality is typically framed in Western psychology. Accurately representing it demonstrates cultural respect and conceptual precision.
items.example: The belief that ancestors provide guidance during difficult moments gives community members a sense of being protected and purposeful, contributing directly to their emotional and spiritual wellbeing.

items.title: I can explain the role of social, historical, and political determinants in the SEWB framework
items.what: The SEWB framework acknowledges that all seven dimensions of wellbeing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are impacted by social determinants (circumstances of living and working), historical determinants (legacy of colonisation and past policies), and political determinants (distribution of power and resources).
items.why: These determinants contextualise individual wellbeing within broader systemic forces. Ignoring them produces an incomplete understanding of SEWB and reflects a lack of critical awareness expected at VCE level.
items.example: The historical removal of Aboriginal children from their families (Stolen Generations) is a historical determinant that continues to affect Connection to Family and Kinship, Community, Culture, and Country for many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people today.

items.title: I can explain why the SEWB framework reflects a collectivist perspective
items.what: The SEWB framework is grounded in a collectivist worldview, meaning the self is understood as significantly linked to family and community rather than as a primarily independent individual. Cultural identity and connection to community are integral to wellbeing in this framework.
items.why: Understanding the collectivist foundation distinguishes the SEWB framework from many Western wellbeing models and explains why dimensions such as Family and Kinship and Community are central rather than peripheral.
items.example: In the SEWB framework, caring for an ill relative is understood as the responsibility of the wider family and community group, not just a biological parent or child. This reflects how wellbeing is communal and relational, not only personal.

items.title: I can explain why the SEWB framework acknowledges diversity within Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
items.what: There is immense cultural and linguistic diversity among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Different groups and individuals may understand social and emotional wellbeing differently. The SEWB framework provides a broad shared structure while acknowledging this diversity.
items.why: Assuming all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples share identical beliefs is inaccurate and culturally disrespectful. This nuance is important for exam responses that discuss the framework's scope and limitations.
items.example: A student living in a remote community in the Northern Territory and an urban Aboriginal person in Melbourne may both draw on the SEWB framework but experience its dimensions very differently depending on their language group, proximity to Country, and access to community structures.
